Volume II January 23, 1941 Number 13 OC JOINS HOSTELS The Outing Club has associated itself with the American Youth Hostels, and members may now enjoy the privilege of using the chain of hostels in various parts of the country. The majority of these units operate only during the summer months, but a number situated in the ski country remain open the year 'round, and the Club looks forward to making good use of such resorts. The New England chains represent the oldest hostels in the U. S., the units customarily be- ing located in farmhouses, and maintaining a tradition of friendli- ness and helpfulness. The "customers" must provide only a sleeping sack, sheet, or blanket, are entitled to beds, blankets, and cook- ing and washing facilities for the nominal 35 cent-per-night fee. MID-YEAR HOSTEL TRIP During the mid-year lull, the OC will remain open for busi- ness for the benefit of the "shut-ins". Among several attractive trips being offered is an eight-day excursion to the snow-country hostels, probable stops being at Guilford and Stowe, and perhaps at Plymouth, N. H. All of these resorts offer unparalleled condittons for skiers, while total expenses for the week should not exceed the very modest sum of ten dollars. The outing is scheduled to depart Saturday, Feb. lst, following exams, and will return Sunday night, a week later. DATE DANCE On Saturday night, January llth, 32 couples merrily banzed a- way at the floor of the Hangar Gym, to the rhythm furnished by Mike Freuhn's corny music-makers. In the interims between dances, five gallons of hot chocolate went down the hatch, attesting to the fine enthusiasm shown by the dancers. Another square dance is carded on the lst of March, and Manager Bill Welch is hankerin! to know wheth- er his constituents would prefer to dig up their own dates, or if they prefer the easier course of having the gals furnished thru the grace of the OC. Bill is also curious to know if the dancers! feet respond more readily to recorded corn than to that produced on the Spot. All those who have opinions to express may do so by writing Bill Welch, M. I. T. Dorms, or by leaving a note in the OC office.

Here are the details: We are planning a weekend of fun on Saturday and Sunday, February 22nd and 23rd, at the American Youth Hostel in Northfield, Mass. The trip will be held jointly with Mt. Holyoke and Smith colleges, and the gang will get together up there at the hostel. The Tech contingent will leave Walker sometime on Saturday morning, and arrive at Northfielc about noon for lunch - we'll meet the girls up there. In the afternoon there will be plenty of fun, skiing, skating, hiking, lots of activity to choose from, and divided up so that the novices will have a fine time, too. In the evening, after a big dinner, a bang-up square dance, with plenty of squares and popular rounds to satisfy everybody. Then singing around the fire, and marshmallows before bed. Next morning, plenty more outing fun, and horseback riding for those who would like to try it - lots of nice trails around. After a good morning's fun, a big lunch, and then home. Let's see a big turnout, and make this the biggest and best Outing Club affair yet! Let's make our fifth anniversary something worth remembering!! --000--

The party will meke use of the stables at the Blue Hills Reservation, where mounts are available at reasonable prices, and the bridle paths have been found to be excellent. Ski enthusiasts from leading schools of the Boston aree will participate in the outing, which is to leave North Station at 7:45 on Sunday morning. Jackson, Tufts, Harvard, Wellesley, Radcliffe, Pine Manor, Simmons, and Sargent are expected to turn out in full force, and there will be plenty of opportunity for social contacts to be made while the train is under way. The price of the trip is only $2.75, and the prospects for snow are good, so put this outing on your "must" list. WHAT HO, SARGENT! A group of about ten Tech men will join a like number of Sargeni girls in a joint trip to Professor Dean Peabody's farm, near Hubbards— ton, Mass., over the week-end of March 15th-16th. The party will part from Technology at 1:30 on Saturday and arrive back in Boston at 6 PM, the following evening. Expenses are expected to be about $1.50. Sat— urday night will be occupied in square dancing, if possible, and there will be skiing on Sunday on Mt. Wachusett or Mt. Monadnock if the snow conditions permit. With brief intermissions in the heated cabin that is available for pur- poses of thawing out, the group remained on the pond until night-fall. Leader Bob Brown expressed himself as entirely satisfied with the pond as a site for skating, and if any interest is displayed, this first trip certainly will not be the last. SPRING! with the advent of March, Spring cannot be far behind. In spite of the fact that the skiers still claim the head-lines, the time is at hand for you rock climbers and canoers to get your equipment out of the moth-balls!

This or- ganization, which was formed in 1923 to fill the need of city people for outdoor recreation, is extending to all interested OC members an opportunity to become acquainted with the activities of the club. A letter addressed to the Chairman of the Membership Committee, Mrs. G. A. Lenaghen, 269 Chestnut Street, Nutley, N. A splendid opportunity for Outing Clubers to follow their hobby after graduation exists, and it is to be hoped that many of them will take advantage of this. CYCLISTS FIND TREASURE TROVE The source of those colorful neckties which have been adorning the upper halves of certain OC men has at last come to light. Oddly enough, it seems that the U.S. Post Office in South Natick is respon- sible for the atrocities. Walter Wells'sbike trip, on March sOth, made the discovery in the course of a forty-seven mile loop which in- cluded Walden Pond, Wellesley, and 8. Natick. The boys stopped off at Walden for lunch and again at the Post Office; we think that they should only have stopped once. SPRING SKI TRIP Eighteen men participated in the vacation ski outing at Gorham. Bill Johnson, leader of the trip, reports that the group enjoyed per- fect weather conditions and fine skiing in Tuckerman's Ravine and on Cannon Mountain. Several men climbed to the summit of Mt. Washington and visited the radio station and meteorological observatory located there, while all hands attained a considerable degree of sunburn.

A lot of blank " pages, Now we come to the point of this little discourse, All _— members are urged to take cameras along on trips AND to take pictures while on said trips. The OC will pay for prints to put in the scrapbook and will take practically anything it can get in the way of trip pictures. Preferably, pictures should show OC members as woll as scenery, If you have taken any pictures on trips, turn them in as soon as possible.
1jr2EMJXPCMT750AZvZuf1dgUTEuEzbPy: Nov. 2, 1942 ANNUAL ELECTION MEETING; Because of the early graduation of the Seniors thie year, the usual March Elections Meeting will beheld on November 18. It will be held at 5 PM in a room to be announced later. The first of what 1s hoped to be a series of ski movies will be shown at this meeting. The manner of elections 168 as follows. The present council will choose men whom they feel will be capable of filling each job well. This list of men will be offered to the members at the meeting. The ballot may be altered by nominations from the floor, in which case a vote will be taken for the position in question. The whole list as presented by the council may also be accepted by one vote if there are no nominations. Selections for positions by the council are based on knowl- edge of the work to be done and on the personal capabilities of the men. Be sure that you know the duties of the posi- tion and the capabilities of a man before you nominate him for any position. Be sure and come out for this meeting and find out who your new officers are. You will also see some good ski movies. RIDING TRIP: There will be a riding trip in the Blue Hills on Sat- urday, November 7. Party will probably leave from in front of Walker about 1 or 2 PM. On riding trips, it is custom- ary for the members going to decide the length of the trip and therefore the cost. Indicate your choice of time on the signup sheet. Signup will go up on Tuesday, November 5. Now is the time to go riding when the air is crisp and the woods are beautiful. ROCK CLIMBING TRIP: On Sunday, November 8, there will be a rock climbing trip, probably to Rattlesnake Cliffs. The OC is trying to develop some leaders for future rock climbing trips so everybody is invited to come out for instruction. Rock climbing is one type of trip where the leader MUST be a trained and experienced man and the supply of such men seems to be running low. With the graduation of the Senior class, there will be very few good men for next year. Come on out and find out what the sport is about. REMEMBER THOSE PICTURES
1HFv5KOHLoAFVadlutcVfewp6TUBmrFML: Volume IV Nov. 9, 1942 Number 6 SQUARE DANCE NOV. 13: The next Council square dance will be held on Friday, Nov. 13 in the North Hall at Simmons. The quota from Tech will be 30 men. This dance will be for Oyting Club members ONLY. The cost will be 35¢ and refreshments will be served. Al Smith will call and there will be an orchestra this time. The signup list goes up on Mon., Nov. 9. RADCLIFFE IOCA TRIP NOV. 15: On Sunday, Nov. 15, a party from Tech will bicycle 22 miles out to Ashland where they will meet the girls from Radcliffe, who will go by train. Lunch will be served at 12:45 by Radcliffe for a small fee of 50¢. We will leave Walker at 9 AM and return in the evening. Signup is already up. BIKE TRIP WITH WELLESLEY: There will be a bike trip with Wellesley on Sunday, Nov. 22. We will leave Walker at 9 AM and return by 6 PM. Wellesley will furnish the lunch at slight cost. YWCA SQUARE DANCES: Al Smith will call for square dancing every Tuesday from 8 to 10 in the YWCA on Clarendon St. in Boston. That is right in back of the Copley Plaza Hotel. The cost will be 50¢ per couple. Come on over and have some fun at these dances. SKI TROOPS: Jimmy Klein, Ski Team Manager, says that he has blanks and information for the 47th Mountain Regiment which is the Ski Troopers outfit. Anyone who would rather get in this than be drafted should see Jimmy at 85 Phillips St., Boston. WELLESLEY TRIP A BIG SUCCESS: 36 men from Tech went out to Wellesley in 2 groups on Sat., Oct. 31. We swam, canoed, played softball, etc. until 5:50 when we gathered for an outdoor supper cooked by the girls with Shriers assistance on the hamburgs. After supper we sang until everybody was hoarse and also saw some IOCA movies. The Tech, Harvard, Radcliffe, and Sargent contingents commandeered a whole car on the ride back, REMEMBER THE MEETING ON NOVEMBER 18 FOR ELECTION OF OFFICERS
18Fn7DPQWUiD1SctXC-CvgnhJk6anfXaJ: Volume IV November 16, 1942 Number 7 SPECIAL _ SPECIAL - SPECIAL SPECIAL ELECTIONS MEETING NOVEMBER 18: The Fall meeting for the election of Outing Club officers will be held at 5 PM, Wednesday, November 18 in Room 1-390. After the elections part of the meeting is completed, we will see two color movies on ski- ing. These will be; "Skiing in the Canadian Rockies" "Unexplored Slopes in New England" Both of these movies should be very good and all members are urged to come and see them. We would like to discourage non-members from com- ing to this meeting because it is hard to hold the elections when there are a large number of non-members present. There will be another open meeting with ski movies in a couple of weeks to which anyone may come. After several weeks deliberation and consideration, the Council has arrived at the following list of candidates for the next Council. It is to be emphasized that further nominations can be made from the floor at the meeting and that the elections will then be held on a majority basis. The men on this list, however, have been carefully chosen on the basis of OC activity and capability for the position. They have also been balanced among the classes so as to have some experienced men for higher office in following years. Here is our list: For Pres. ~ Bill van Ravenswaay (present Sec.-Treas. '44. Sec.-Treas. — Oiva Anderson, '45 Trips Director — Cy Kano, '43 Meetings Director - Joe Shrier, '44 OC News Editor ~ George Werner, '45 Ski Team Mgr. - Jimmy Klein, '43 Be sure and come out for this meeting, both to elect your new officers and to see some fine ski movies. WELLESLEY BIKE TRIP NOV. 22: If you hurry, you can still get on the list for the bike trip with Wellesley, November 22. See board for details.
1vpD3s0fFaHaXZaq4-ETdsNXCcQe7nKpF: MUTI CLUS SS) Volume IV November 23, 1942 ELECTION RESULTS: The annual election meeting was held on November 18 in Room 1-390. The list of men approved by the old Council was accepted and there were no further nominations. The new Council was then unanimously elected as a whole. Your officers for next year are as follows: President - Bill van Ravenswaay, '44 - 22 The Fenway, Boston. Sec.-Treas. - Oiva Anderson, '45, 60 Washington Elms, Cambridge. Meetings Director Cy Kano, '43 212 Graduate House. Trips Director - Joe Shrier, '44 ~ Munroe 506, Dorms. OC NEWS Editor - George Werner, '45 — 40 Hereford Street, Boston. Ski Team Mer. - Jimmy Klein, '43 85 Phillips Street, Boston. These men will take over direction of the OC next week, although the old bunch will probably hang around for a week or so until the new outfit gets well started, Good luck! Members attending this meeting also saw two ski movies in color; "Unexplored Slopes in New England," and "Skiing in the Canadian Rockies." The first picture showed some scenes that were familiar to some of the members present and also some scenes that were not familiar, such as some of Presidential Range slopes that are not usually skied on. SKI MEETING ON WEDNESDAY, DEC. 2: , Jimmy Klein, Ski Team Manager, has announced a special ski meeting to be held in Room 1-390 at 5 PM on Wednesday, Dec. 2. There will be some colored movies of skiing that have not been shown to the OC before and it will be worth while to come out and see these. The meeting is open to anybody that wants to come and all men at all interested in the ski team are urged to attend. Jimmy has a pretty good program lined up for the team this year, despite the war conditions and would like to talk to every man who is interested in the team. EDITORIAL COMMENT: The new editor, George Werner, will take over the NEWS next week and we pause here to wish him luck. It has been a lot of fun putting out the NEWS for the last year and we hope that George will have as much. Of course, there are times when we have wished that we could forget it for a week or so but that was when we were Just too busy with something else. Guess that it is George's turn now. John Ward, '43 - Retiring Editor.

The spiders who went scrambling over Joe English Cliffs had a thoroughly enjoyable time last week, All the usual climbs were done with the exception of the Balcony Route and a couple of others which were not dry enough. Bernie Burke and Jim eorer both led the liilk Route, the Pipe-line was led by Burke, snd Towle's Terror by Phil Morrow. Others present were Dave Lull and Peul Westheimer. An interesting incident which later caused a lot of chuckles but at the time didn't seem particularly funny was when Lull and Morrow started climbing what they thought was the Thin Air Route. After considerable straining ant audible grunting they reached the lofty height of about 100 feet only to run into a profound scarcity of holds of eny_kind. That is when they began to wonder whether they "were on the Thin Air Route or really in thin air. After another 10 feet or so they concluded that the latter was the case. By going through various seemingly impossible contortions and resorting to every sort of trick with the exception of the use of suction cups they managed to drive in a piton, improvise a rope carabiner, and rappel down with smouldering trousers and shoulders. NEWS a : ANNUAL REPORT 1948-49 During the past two terms, the MITOC NEWS (official organ of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Outing Club) was published in mimeographed form and distributed by either Institute or U.S. Mail to the members and patrons of the above mentioned organizatsz ion. It was also sent to all other Outing Clubs in the New England area (plus a few of the larger clubs in the neighboring Northeast- ern 8tates. The purpose of this publication is to present NEWS to MITOC members. When there is insufficient material in the way of trip dope and announcements, the sheet is filled with items of general interest or, and this is usually the case, pure unadulterated bull.(hence the expression 'bull-sheet' The MITOC "EWS prides itself on its original mastheads. In the absence of a staff artist, they have been drawrby the editors (darn good jobs, some of them, too). Anyone who feels inclined is encouraged to dream up a head, but the editors reserve the right to accept or reject them as they see fit. One of the editors' mos t difficult tasks is that of operating the mimeo machine - it is very temperamental. May whoever wished the in- fernal guck heap on the Outing Club rot in his bed! . Up to date mailing lists must be maintained. Separate lists for Dorms, Grad House, Barracks, Institute, and Commuters should be made, Addressing the News is the most tedious job, that is, if left for one or two people. If several volunteers take on the job regularly, it is no trouble at all. This also insures prompt mailing. The approximate cost per weekly issue (including mailing) is $8.50. Co Mas bf Giles NEWS Co-Editorg 1948-49 This is paid by membership dues.

Again this year MITOC is running its annual [OCA triv to Katahdin for the Thanksgiving vacation, This is a rugged Winter mountaineering trip. The weather on Katahdin, in nortnern Maine, May be extreme by late November, We could get anything from 40° and sunny days to 30 mph winds, snow, and temperauvures well below freezing. To quote from Tom Lehre, "Be prepared." All clubs should be sure that their gro 7p has had some previous experience in comping out under cold weather conditions. Those traveling with MITOC will be required to go on one of the conditioning trips, either Oct 26-23 to Imp Shelter or Nov 9-12 to the Mahoosucks. The general run of events goes like this. Wed night drive to Roaring Brook camp ground at the foot of Mt. Katahdin Thur morning hike to Chimney Pond. Here you are permitted to collapse for the rest of the day. You will probably want to get up for dinner though. A complete Thanksgiving dinner with turtey and all the trimmings will be served to everyone by MITOC. Fri and Sat are for sacking out, eating, climbing, Snow ball throwing, goofing, song festing, ete. Sunday wiil bring more of the same, and a walk back to the cars and return to home. dé Tt's a 3.2 mi pack from the parking lot at Roaring Brook to the Chimney Pond camp ground. Allow at lezst two 'ours for the trip, more if the weather is bad. As usual, the trail is uphill, same as last year, (the milage hasn't changea much either), and hiking in cold weather and snow is far more tiring than traveling a Similar trail in the summer months. Clubs from other schools must provide their own transportation to Katahdin and their own food with the exceotion , of Thurs night. MITOC will provide a complete Thanksgiving . dianer on Thurs. Registration for the trio is $1.00 per oerson which must be in the hands of MITOC by Fri q?, Nov. 16. This small fee is necessary to cover handling and maiiing charges for the turkey dinner. Group Leaders must sign in at the rangers cabin at Cnim- ' ney Pond upon arrival. TRIP REPORT CANOEING The President of this here arganization says we shall write trip reports when we lead trips. UGH Damn his eyeSe The News Editor says the news henceforth shall be mimeographed so I gotta type on a mimeo stencil UGH Damn his eyeSe The President wishes statistics - here they are; Canoe Trip April 7: 22 pecple, 6 cars Canoe Trip April 14: 15 people; 4 cars UGH Now I shall set forth in some illogical style to present pertinent and impertineht facts about these two trips - beware, I am typing from my head to the typewritér - ell errors at your own riske April 7 = "Concord" River. After suitable minor incidents with owners? of boat house in Goncord, we proceeded, somewhat scattered down the Sudbury river and thence up the Assabet. At some leter time we managed to get together - liabilities at this point were one broken paddle (it didn't really matter much - they were lcusy paddles anyway)e Now the water got swifter and people found there were tricks to paddling upstream - as welt as work. Anyhoo, much paddling later found us at the base, or near, of a dam which we carried canoes around end put them in the lake abOVee Another hour or so across the lake and on up the river and we found a suitable spot for lunch? it was now two~-thirty or S06 Also by this time we haa lost three of the original ten canoes. One had to return early - but two vanished without even telling anyone where they were going, for shame. Downstream was more funy, less work, and hastier - six or seven canoes held together make ea nice raft sociable and one or two people can steer it well. Note: the Assabet is a dirty smelly river in spots, pretty in others - but the Sudbury is mostly SwampSApril 14 - Ipswich River. This was indeed interesting - so read on. With usual endless delay it was '10:30 before cars were spotted, canoes acquired, etc. and actual progress started. But from then on the fun began - the river was somewhat flooded, it 4ssmall and very crooked, full of trees, etc., plus some riffles, dams, and so on. And there was quite a bit of current in places which made for entertaining operations. In fact I suspect that now that we have sampled simple white water we siould go back and learn the rules. The morning was relatively simple and uneventful as we twisted and turned our way downstream - exception was one canoe that managed to get swept under a branch and acquire a little water - but occupants stayed drye Incidentally canoes were anctent wood with many broken ribs plus addition of fiber glass and other goo - very heavy and still leaky - but paddles were reasonablé. Lunch in a wooded glen - and then back to the river. Before we left the winding in the trees an absent minded stern man managed to get swept off his seat by a low branch and the ensuing shift of the canoe also dumped the bow lady off - both in four or five feet of water but no water in the canoe; pay attention, doggone it. Later we left the trees and continued the same snake path across open swampland, and since it was sligittly flooded somes decided to shortcut the process - sometimes 4t worked and then again sometimes I'saw some feet in two or three inches of water walking their canoe somewhere. All this open aréa used up another hour or more of our

timee Then the river got larger and everything proceeded nicely for awhile and we traveled on until we came to a dam about three feet high. So we carried around and then it was suggested that noble trip leader, who was first canoe back in, should paddle up to base of dam - big waterfall = so pictures could be taken. All of which went fine until he backed off to go downstream only to find a second dam about two feet high less than 100 feet downstream, Hasty operations were required to miss going where one shouldn't, Damn picture takers, particularly ones who say move further out in the river cause there is no sun where you are. And file on all idiots who don't look downstream before getting back in the river. Ah well, alls well that ends well. Belsw the second dam there were series of whitecapped riffles - all very swift and pretty but at times most disturbing because they would appear suddenly around a bend with no warning. But no incidents either. Later still at a railroad bridge debris had blocked almost all of the river so that the water went through the one remaining opening and dropped a foot or so = swift and delightful once you decided to go through. After this a little ways came the town of Ipswich and the end of the line. We had started in Middleton and paddled or been swept an estimatéd, that is roughly measured, 20 miles of winding, twisting river( It was now five PM. One canoe up on a VW and back to starting point with the drivers to get the other cars. Then back and this time it was a canoe on each of two VW's plus three canoes on Mike's Jeep — Indeed we made an interesting procession on Easter Sunday Afternoon through traffic from Ipswich to Middleton. After that some went home and the rest went to Chinatown to #111 in a decided void, Note: This is a nice river - though might be a problem when water is low. But not for rank begginers - know something about canoeing and the effects of swift current on a canoe MEK. And to revive an ancient trip writer$S cliche which was once banned from these pages: All in all it was a good trip. PEOPLE - I lost track of them all - names that is, but here are wheat I can remember for the two trips: April 7 = 22 People April 14 - 13 People Gardner Perry III Mary perry Gardner Perry III Mary Perry Willie Crowther Pat Page Willie Crowther Pat Page Mike Drooker Penny Ballard Mike Drooker Penny Ballard Bob Gilmore Trini Perry Norm Kasser Myna Kasser - George Lewis Verna Lewis Shelby Hildebrand Nancy Nichols Nancy Lewis Phil Dangel Sam Drake Bill Steffy Marty Maltz Jane Smith Debra Cohen and three more from Wellesley plus five others from MIT I think Is end of writing trip reports for awhile cause I am not leading trips-.for next three wovuks at least - just going. GENERAL INFORWATION: ROCK CLIWBING AND WINTKR MOUNTAINEERING All MITOC trips which involve rock Climbing (other than local top rope climbing trips) or winter (Oct 15 = Apr 15) mountain climbing; dDecause of their inherent complexity, are administered by committees on these activities. The following is a brief resume of how this works and a listing of the various leaders connected with these activities. ROCK CLIMBING: Rock climbers upon becoming known in the group and acguiring certain skills are classified into three groups: seconds, rope leaders, and ARC leaders. The ARC Leaders do the classifying. Any rock climbing trip must have an AIC Leader to supervise the rock climbing. Training of new climbers is solely by permission and supervision of ARC Leaders. Rope Leaders may lead with qualified Seconds or other Leaders, and shoul? inform the trip (ARC) leader of what they are doing. Qualifications are as follows: 1. As a former IOCA Lake George trip leader, 1 feel obliged to point out te those responsible certain facts and results, none of which can be considered amusing. 1) For years the shortage of canoes has been the principal source of difft«ulty in running the Lake George trip. Over one-quarter of the 500 or so participants are brought to the islands by a necessarily irregular motor boat ferry, and must beg, borrow, or steal canocey in order to participate in Biking and other weekend activities. Unfortunately, many canoes are frequently (and understandably) "borrowed" without permiszion, leading to numerova arguments and hard feelings among various IOCA individuals and clubs. The loss of canoes from Mohican Island was generally thought .to be just widespread "borrowing" by individuals, rather than a single prank, thereby accentuating an already sensitive problem. This has contributed to the serious com sideration by some ROC leaders of trying to move or completely cancel future IOGCA Lake George trips. | 2) The greatest source of relief for the canoe-shortag. proolem has been from | & growing practice of individuals and clubs to buy or rent their own canoes and | transport them large distances to Lake George. These groups must go to great lengths | | (Ed. :NB pun. to keep track of their own cances and prevent them from becoming | | mixed up with the RPI-rented canoes from Bolton's Landing. They cannot be expected | to continue going to ali this trouble if they must also spend haif the weekend lecatinag | boats stolen from them. (A large percentage of the beats taken from Mohican Island | | were such private property. ) | 3) Twrtle and the Surrounding isiands are state land. The permit required for | 10C4 Vaik Lake George has been more difficult to obtain each year, due to isolated | cases of moving tables, leaving garbage, burning unauthorized fires, chopping up docks for firewood, etc. Cutting down a sapling in order to remove a cance chained to it, ' as part of a4 practical joke, is act a good way to make friends with the rangers. | 4) Certain members of the RFI Outing Club spend all weekend working for IQCA, | registering people, runming motor boats, preparing the square dance area, etc., and wasting very 1littla time cating, sleeping, or otherwise enjoying the weekend. ._ = OCOMUMBUS DAY WEEKEND AT BIGELOW be ' On the weekend of October 12th, Doc Edesses, Pete Cleveland, Jim Powers, sam Drake, and Philip Dangel climbed Cranberry Peak, North and South Horn, Bigelow, Avery Peak, and Little Bigelow. Doc, Jim, and Pete left in the VW at four; Sam and Phil left in the jalopy at six, after supper. The jalopy was extremely noisy and spouted purple flames through a hole in the exhaust crossover. It was also, except for a windshield, completely open, and guzzled gasoline like a dinosaur. We filled ic up and goosed out, leaving behind a big cloud of exhaust and a few shattered windows. At the beginning of the Maine Turnpike we picked up two hitchhikers bound for Lewiston, but they implored us te discharge them at the next exit, forty miles short of their destimation. We did so graciously. Shortly thereafter the fan belt broke, causing the engine to quit while we were passing someone at high speed. Replacing it with a piece of clothesline, we made it out to a gas station in Sewth Portland. The delay was only thirty minutes. Pate impelled us rapidly northward, up routes & and 27 to Kingfield, where we met the VW at 11.30. For the benefit of the Kingfield residents we goosed ovt again. The entire world, silenced by the roar of the heap was bathed in the eerie light of a half moon. Dead leaves blew slowly across the road, and the Carrabasset River, beside which route 27 runs north of Kingfield, hooked more like an apparition than a reality. At 1.30 we bedded down @ Jerome Brook Shelter, in the middle of a desolate, subarctic marshland. Swaser had indeed ended. Saturday morning was spent spotting cars. Jim, Doc, and Pete swore they would never ride in the back of that cut down pickup truck again. The purpose of the trip had originally been to blaze a trail for a winter trip, but this Curmed owt to be an impossible tesk because of the condition of the trail. Lunch oa Cranberry Peak at 1.30 was a chilling experience, and the Horns were covered with snow and quite forbidding. Progress was unbelievably slow. "Maine can sure stretch out « mile," Pete commented wryly. Washington, 8Omiles away, we left in as much — of e hurry és we could. Just before daxk we got out of the woods (at four) and drove the VW eround to Stratton, Maine where the jalopy was waiting. We divided again into two groups, but this time we went back in convoy, because Sam was afraid that the jalopy might not make it. Aft the junction of routes 2 and 4 there was a horrible clanking, audible to those inside the VW 300 yards behind. Then it happened...it soon became apparent that the jalopy had thrown a rod and would have to sbandoned on the spot. The five of us piled into the WW and notified the police, who said they would tow it to a garage the next day. We didn't get home until three the next morning (Monday), but it was a great trip. Since then Saw and the owner of the jalopy, Ray Vaughan, have made a pilgrimage to Borth Jay, Maine to fix the heap. This weekend Drooker might tow it back where it will be reactivated; the repairs should cost enly about $10--end a lot of time. (The heap only cost 650 originally, and the garage owner had offered Ray $5 for it in its sadly fallen state.) -Phil Dangel

Monadnock, I observed a large number of very wild~looking peoples from the wilds of Camslumbridge National Dump invading our peaceful, civilized comumunity in large, chugging imitation beetles from B1f land. Some peoples also came in a monster from the Detroit Wilds, and others in a midget monster. At the end of the peoplemonster trail the pseudobeetles and the |onsters vere left behind, the peoples put on initation snowshoes, ai.d the herd started up the mountain. One people put on a long flat stick on each foot instead of an imitation snowshoe. Peoples were cheated by nature when they got such silly-looking bodies; and only two legs! t considered offering carrots to some off the peoples, especially Since some of them needed something of the sort, and the wild food they had didn't look very appetizing, but I remenbered the rule asainst feeding the peoples and didn't. I decided to stay out of sight, so es to not scare the peoples away, and observe their habits. It was easy to stay out of sight, since peoples are very slow and clumsy, and are very unobservant. Since other peoples had been up the trail previously, the peoples did not need to wear imitation snowshoes if they stayed on the trail, and many of them took the imitation snowshoes off and carried tiem the rest of the way when they came to the steep part of tle trail, but some peoples wore imitation snowshoes all the way, since this was a beginr.ers' snowshoe trip. Some of the peoples put imitation claws on their feet, while the others just slid and spun with the wind. EDITORIAL ON TOCA | Since most MITOC members probably don't know what IOCA is, we | have decided to include in this issue a rather complete account of the , recent [OCA Conference held at Samp Howe:. V'e hofe that by reading-the proceedings, you will take.an interest in being a part of them next year, or at the very least, learn what IOCA is all about. For all of you who are absolutely unable to wrench yourself away from your books long enough to read the following reports, perhaps this short description will do. IOCA (that's Intercollegiate Outing Club Association, stupid) is composed of about 40 member clubs, which through regional committees (we're in Eastern New England division) cooperate on the running . of trips. There' | Unfortunately MIT isn't very active in IOCA affairs. I believe that the reason for this is that we have an unusually active, self-sufficient club. Outing clubs will naturally tend to cooperate among themselves mosf when | by doing so they benefit each other by bolstering weaknesses such as lack of transportation, trim leaders or members to participate. MITOC is rela- : tively free from these problems. This does not prohibit our being of help in ENEC (Eastern N. England Counci} - but here for the most part, clubs are either strong enough to stand on their own feet or so distant as to prohibit close coordination in running trips. Of course, none of this makes an interchange of ideas and information impossible. This may be accomplished by IOCA Bulletins, Regional Newsletters, or the IOCA Conference. Here I have some concrete suggestions - more newsletters and bulletins, and distribution of an IOCA - compiled directory of member outing club officers and their addresses to facilitate communication. The IOCA Conference as it stands is very worthwhile. One point - much time could be saved if discussion leaders exercised more active control by guiding conversation away from irreleven: and obviously trivial matters. | Finally, no evaluation of IOCA and the IOCA Conference would be complete without a tip of the hat to Smith Outing Club (sponscrs of the Conference). They efficiently handled matters from accomodations and. scheduling to the smallest administrative detail. Thanx to Smith for a hard job well-done! (Even if they did make us wash dishes at the last minute). Pre-Circus Cookie-fest ae Tom Greytak ) Marty Maltz Brian Mokler Ann S.cattergood Dave Freifelder a aie Lee Dennison : Ferren MacIntyre | \ The Outing Club cookie is a concept which is just beginning to emerge and it still has a long way to go to reach the "tradition" stage. The nucleus of the movement was prolebly a wastebasket of dinner plate sized chocolate chip cookies that Willie (C.) took toa Taylor song-fest a ways back. The Dana Street Bakery has done its best to experiment and classify. We recognize four standard sizes: Breakfast - 4" diameter, lunch - 6" diameter, dinner - 8" diameter, and lecture size which are rejects that will fit in a shirt pocket until one gets nungry during a session on electron-nucleon scattering. We chose chocolate chip and oatmeal cookies in the lunch size for the circus. Desiring about 120 cookies in all, we used as a base 8 times the recipe on the oatmeal box and 8 times that on the chocolate chip bag. The batter for each of the two types filled two standard dishpans; the lunch size meant six cookies per : cookie sheet. We suggest for anyone planning an undertaking of similar magnitude that the n people throwing raw materials into the pot keep up some sort of communication to avoid problems of duplication or omission, and by all means, remember which cookies are being made in eac!: pot. Circus Hike - Mount Monadnock | Dave Freifelder Don Silversmith Karl Norstrom Harold Solomon | Bary Laux Judy Scott Anne Norton Ira Turner + | 4 Johathan (Harvard) : ) , Kathy (Radcliffe) | ) No trip seems to be possible without some confusion. I guess daylight saving time didn't help either. Wasn't too bad though - of the four | people who weren't on the trip, as far as I know, there was only one who missed out because of either misinformation or confusion. At any rate, we left Walker only 45 minutes late, having picked up a new trip member who came for the canoe trip but hadn't thought it necessary to sign up in advance. We reached Mt. Monadnock only to find the state park, and therefore certain counted-on facilities, closed. More distressing, though, was that the car with the Wellesley girl which presumably had left on time was not there. : After 15 minutes we decided to start up and left a rather conspicuous note on the assumption that they had not already started up without us. It was a beautiful hike up. Because of the lack of rain, the trail was completely dry; unfortunately spring had not yet arrived so there was no greenery. It was sunny and clear and only chilly when we stood still. We reached the top in about two hours (White Dot Trail) having eaten some nice clean snow on the | way. The missing group arrived about fifteen minutes later and of course had never seen our note. We had lunch and descended the White Cross trail and returned to a welcome Glop bucket via an even more welcome ice cream stand. The Upper Charles River Revisited ~ aaa "But Gardener'. Executive Committee Meeting Tomtack It became clear at the IOCA Conference that MITOC is one of the largest and most active clubs in IOCA. It is not surprising, then, that one of the problems that has prompted quite a bit of discussion in the club seems to be unique to MITOC. This problem is the maint.e nance and rental of our relatively large amount of equipment. The greatest portion of the technical (red tape or administrative, if you will) part of running the club centers about the equipment problem - repair, holding office hours so that it may be rented and picked up, tracking down unreturned equipment and fighting the battle of the reservation sheet. This has not been unprofitable; in fact we have made an embarrassingly substantial profit considering that equipment rental was supposed to be a break-even service to members. The question that was considered by the committee was to what extent does our present rental policy implement the central purpose of the Outing Club - that is, to be a center for activities and trips through which interested people can enjoy the outdoors. We decided that the club has probably gone farther into the rental business than is necessary and haveset up a new rental policy: EQUIPMENT MAY BE RENTED ONLY FOR OFFICIAL OUTING CLUB TRIPS. We do not think that this is a golden solution: its drawbacks were discussed at length as were some of its advantages. Some clarifying comments should be made, however. a. If, after a suitable trial period, the policy seems to be detrimental to the club, it can be revoked. b. The trip need not be a MITOC trip; other IOCA trips as well as AMC and Sub Sig are accepted. c. The primary effect will be on ski rental, but as it stands now, one may rent good, if not better, ski equipment at the slopes for comparable prices. d. Official trips are not hard to come by and except for the following . reasonable exceptions anyone may organize a MITOC trip. Winter mountaineering and rock climbing leaders, because of the dangers involved, must be approved by the appropriate committee. Cabin leaders should have a working knowledge of the cabin and therefore must have the permission of the cabin manager. Mike Drooker gave an estimate of the cost of adding a 15' x 15' kitchen wing tothe cabin. It would be located south of the present kitchen and would lead to smoother functioning of the cabin on trips of over 20 people. The cost would be about $700 and the project would require at least six weekend work trips: No decision was made on the project since the song sheet is also showing §19ns of life and if undertaken, would require a substantial capital investment: We are having 2 Slide show along with our usual display:of unusual equipment and ethnic people at the Freshmen Activities Midway on Friday night, September 20th» in Rockwell Cage. Do come and seduce freshmen if you can add to the entertainment. There will be sign-up sheets for several trips the following Sunday' if you would like to lead one - all the better.

GORP - - - By Ferren Gorp is a food known and beloved by ground squirrels, mountaineers, and marmots throughout the land. 'It achieved its fame 'even in its Dark Ages, before its renaissance under the skilled chemistry of MITOC's resident oceanographer, when it reached its present and laudable gustatory excellence, Designed to sustain life (if not exactly able to create an interest in maintaining life), gorp is an ideal back-packing food. Two pounds will supply the calories for a day of strenous effort, while furnishing also the protein, vitamins, and minerals which the body needs. It is non-perishable (though it deteriorates aesthetically as the chemical potential of water in the components reaches equilibrium), non-squashable, and can be used as insulation under a sleeping bag withovc 111 effect. It combines quick-energy carbohydrates with a well-balanced combi-~ nation of protein and fat, which are digested but slowly, giving one a feeling of post-prandial contentment which lasts for miles, Once upon a time, "gorp" was merely an assortment of ral+ sins, Toll House bits, and that aberrant desicated legume, the goober, or ground nut. This assemblage, this unselected concatenation of left-overs from the previous tenant's child's fourth birthday party, this barrelscraping admission of insolvency, this uninspired miscegenation of unpalatability - - this, I say, was sufficient to keep body and soul together in man and beast. Pulled from a pocket (or stolen from a pack) it was held gingerly in the fingers (paws) and nibbled carefully in an effort to keep the mashed and melted chocolate out of the whiskers (vibrissae). Its taste was that of a stale candy bar filched from an abandoned vending machine, I ask the reader now to suspend disbelief, for I must report that such ill conceived fare has been known to inspire hand-to-hand and hand-to-paw combats over its distribution, That this execrable rubbish should produce similar reactions in species as diverse as M. marmota and H. neanderthalensis only points up our inability to extrapolate the behavior of these mammals in the civilized laboratory to their behavior under the anozia and tourist plague, found where marmot and mountaineer meet face to hairy face. As part of MITOC's unceasing program to make the mountains more enjoyable to those who by ecological niche or chronic unemployment must live there, we present the first recipe for a palatable gorp. EDIBLE GORP Macadamia nuts, Cashews, Brazil nuts, dried nectarines, dried sour cherries, Monukka seedless raisins (NOT Thompson seedless? Thuri dates (NOT hydrated Deglet Noors! Thuri's are the "bread date" of the Bible, and together with camel's milk, will keep

an arab alive interminably, There are 49 trees in Coachella Valley, and I personally consume a quarter of a tree-crop, so let's not get carried away with enthusiasm!) The last ingredient is tropical chocolate (It really doesn't melt), To this sound base can be added randomly walnuts, almonds , dried pears, figs, filberts, dried apples, dried bannanas, cooked chesnuts, and lichee nut meats, Peanuts ia a comic strip, and under International Copyright Law cannot be included in gorp.

We were Climbing in a dull grey cloud, plodding methodically upward in yesterday's steps; when a break in the clouds afforded a glimpse of the valley floor. Lit by a completely colorless brilliance, each feature stood out in sharp relief in an unearthly panorama. One had the rare experience of seeing something totally new - an experience normally available only when we're too young to appreciate its wonder, and whose recollection is lost in growing up. Fora brief moment, Franconia Notch existed nascent and unrelated to the real world, a preternatural mescaline glimpse into the set of worlds-thatmight-have-been. And then the cloud closed in, leaving behind the ache that accompanies beauty unshared with the right person. --Ferren MacIntyre TRIP REPORT - Wellesley Square Dance - Saturday, Aprii 11 When my carload reached Wellesley at about 8:30, there were @ total of about l2 fellows from MITOC, about a half-dozen other rellows, and two giris, one of whom was taking ticket money. TRIP REPORTS Nature cooperated extraordinarily well with Bill Alves, Don Nelson, and me (Michael Froman) on our March 26 Franconia Traverse. We left Cambridge at 3:15 A.M. under a full moon and cloudless sky and asrived at Lafayette Place by 6:30 (we spent i/2 hour fixing a misassembled Car jack so that we could fix a flat tire). The first fortuitous circumstance was a morning temperature cold ehough so the snow was hard enough for us to walk up Lafayette (via the Old Bridal Path) without snowshoes, and thus save both energy and time. By the time we had reached the Greenieaf Hut and had passed the deep snow, the sun was bright, the temperature up in the 40's and the snow soft. The second gift of «ture was visibility on the order of 100 miles coupled with superb views from the ridges. The third gift was the absence of wind throughout the entire traverse {except for a few 20 mph gusts on the summit of Lafayette). We walked as far as Mt. Liberty and then descended via the Liberty Spring and Whitehouse Tralls. One of the interesting sights of the trip was a huge snow cornice on the ridge between Little Haystack and Ltberty. Don Nelsen has beautiful color slides to document the trip. Mike Froman Spring was here the first week in April. How do I know? Stowe, Madonna, Glen Ellen, Sugar Bush, etc decided to close for the season. 20 hardy souls (a phrase often used by OC'ers) decided notto go to the Spring Ski Festival. A quick call to the U.V.M. lodge confirmed these opinions for Northern Vermont. On April 6th and 7th, snow finally came. Killington seemed to have the best condittons. Friday night I decided to go skilng, made a few phone calls, and filled my Avanti with Linda Up-:on, Claus-Szerbesko, and Steve Strickler. We left Saturday morning 5:80 A.M. and arrived at Killington at 8. The mountain was in the clouds, 30 F, and had 9 inches of winter powder. We skied in the fog till 11:00. When the fog lifted we had excellent spring skiing and sun tans. We leit Killington at 5:00 and were home by 8:30. Jon Morey Saturday, April 22, was a typrical New England Spring day: Cold, raingy and raw. But we five, Tony larrobino, Carmel Carvaro, Craig Banis, Mike Froman, and I hopefully started our canoe trip. We arrived at the Charles River about 11:00, with damp hazy weather but no rain. We started in South Natick by the dam and steadily plowed along against the current for three miles as far as the bridge. Our de'e'mination paid off; as usual the

. as weatherman was wrong and we had a beatulful clear day. We took Lime out to do a Little nature hunting, picking mushrooms and pussy willows, When we had lunch. Fairly tired, we took a leisurely glide back enjoying the colonlal and modern houses that lined the banks; the current was strong enough to propel us with a minimum of effort. Cleaning the muddy debris off the canoes bothered us for 6 while but after we tied the canoes back on Tony's oar the weatherman was proved right. It poured as we wearily drove home. The eveni, the December 16-17 beginners' death-march...well, that is, the leader appears to have known what the trip wassto be, but he was careful to conceal his intent from the rest of the party, until that dramatic moment. "Oops, missed the trail. Well, let's take the next one." The we consists of Ed Grew, Paul Langacker, Bob Pratt, Don Rolph, Iouise V/ilson, and I think there was naother guy. the name seems to have slipped away. Aside from two of the group who sneaked off after a good night's sleep from somewhere north of Boston, we gathered punctually at the Student Center at 5 a.m. and promptly. well, we did get going. At about 9 a.m. we crept out of the warm nests of metal we brought with us from Boston and entered that wonderland of snow, ice, wind, and cold that was to be our home for a couple of days (at least that was all we had planned on After a few rapid pack adjustments, we quickly spotted cars and. sat down to wait about an hour so that it wouldn't seem like we were rushing into this thing. After all, the 10° temp and 30mph winds in the notch weren't that encouraging. When we were finally so cold that we could hardly move, Tony announced that he was ready, and we Started up the trail. It was purely with the hope of regaining our body heat that we ever got into this thing. About 3 hours later we arrived at Greenleaf Hut, laden with tents, stoves, pots, sleepers, clothes, food, an extra pair of K-boots (had we met anyone on the mountain, we might have been able to rentithem), and heavenknows-what in that short stubby bright-colored pack belonging toA. What happened to that extra hour?" So we ate our Lipton Chicken Baronet glop and Beef Stroganoff soup (always end up with too much water), let darkness arrive, and contemplated sleep. "But surely we need some exercise. Let's build an igloo." So some of us tried. We actually got one layer plus a few blocks of a second layer placed before we tired of that game. Maybe it's'that business of notching the blocks to fit them together that made them keep crumbling up as we struggled to place them securely, eh Tony? By 6:30 a.m. we somehow managed to open our eyes to the beautiful sun (above the light local cloud cap) and the 4" new snowcover. Then, after a quick breakfast glop and some speedy dishwashing, we tore down our tents, rapidly stuffed everything into our packs, and dashed on our Crampons. "But let's clean up camp before leaving. Raymond Cataract I Nov. ll, 1967 "We're on an island, that's the trouble." "Land ahead." "We're on a trail!" "I just want to get out of here the fastest way." "This is the Only way to hike, straight up the mountain - none of those trails." (An early comment.) At 4A.M. we met at MIT, after breakfast. By 4:15 all hikers - Paul Langacker, Mike Froman, Bob Pratt, Marty Golubitsky, Robin Wilson, Abhay Bhushan, Ed Grew, Don Rolph, Don Hnatowich, Jean Ulrich, Bill Alves and Tony Iarrobino - were en route to Pinkham Notch amid hordes of hunters up for the first open deer weekend. We arrived (some of us) early enough to see the pink alpine glow on Mt. Washington during sunrise. By Pinkham Notch Camp it'd turned white; we drove a half mile further around a curve to One of the best road views of Washington: one sees Boot Spur and Glen Boulder on the left, part of Tuckerman Ravine, Lions Head, our goal Ravine of Raymond Cataract in the middle, and Huntington Ravine on the right, in panorama. After checking Korea boots, flashlights, mittens, wind pants, and face maSks, and distributing 2 winter sleeping bags, down parkas, and 3 quatts of hot cocoa that the group carried, and weighing about 200 lbs. of packs, we started up Tuckerman Trail somewhat late, 8:00. We took the Huntington Ravine Trail, missed the Raymond path, turned around (after getting almost to the Huntington Basin and noticing some walls between us and Raymond Cataract) reaching the HMC cabin again at 10:00 A,M. We decided to cut through open woods to Raymond Cataract, which we did, ascending slightly and finding easy going. We reached the falls at about 10:30. Just before the falls - now pretty much iced over with water underneath - is a grass slope where we stopped to eat and ponder. The Raymond Cataract trip was one I'd wanted to do for a long time; there's an old trail up it, and its North side is billed by AMC as a winter escape route, Since none of us had been up it before, Bill and I had announced a hard hike up Raymond Cataract and down Glen Boulder Trail, noting that we might not evenreach the summit. It'd be an adventure hike, and we only allowed persons we hoped or knew would be in shape or fast. We were eating on the North side, decided to stay there: Abhay Bhushan and Don Rolph found a route upto some giant icicles. The illusion of freedom when we took pictures of each other against the ice fall, broke off icicles, viewed Wildcat, and Boot Spur froma different angle, was just great. Some noticed that the blue skies had clouded over - we expected some snow but reasonable 30-40 mph winds and continued high temperatures of 279-329 F, Then came the crux of the hike - 2 1/2 hours spent swimming about 1/2 to 3/4 mile through 8-11 foot high balsam fir (Mike Froman identified the enemy.) At the start we made the mistake of spreading out quite a bit - five separate bushwacks - but reassembled and stayed together after that. What we'll try next time is keeping close to the Cataract and cutting back to the river bed just above the falls. What we did see to parallel the river bed NE of it (avoiding steep sides and falls I thought might lie on the bed) reaching a rock line, then cut left from its top, reaching another. By then it was 1P.M., several of us were quite tired, and I was privately estimating we'd get down via Alpine Garden Trail and Auto Road to Glen House at about 11 P,M, V/e discussed cutting to Lion's Head (whereupon we would have taken Right Gully to avoid going down the icy parts of LH Trail at night,) but opted for Alpine Garden partly on bushwhacker Ed Grew's advice, partly to avoid LH and RG. We went upthe rock patch, very soon finding some cairns which, however, didn't seem to lead anywhere - maybe

a | D. 2 an old trail. Just as we were leaving them, Bill Alves noticed they were really the cairns marking the turning right "20 yds. before the brook ai re underground" in the guidebook route description. We wnt up the para ee ae rock line, and after a short easy "bushwhack" reached trail, hiked to the - Alpine Garden Trail, and on it past Huntington Ravine to the Nelson ie 2 Trail. There we split. Those continuing to the road were surprised to be 4 = Passed by a car, then a truck. By almost unaminous decision we accepte | the Job Corps kind offer to truck us down. We stopped at the 5 1/2 mile mark briefly for the Nelson Crag group. So four rode down, four walked down the auto road, beating four - Bill Alves, Don Rolph, Abhay Bhushan, and Paul Langacker, who found snow-covered ice on the lower Nelson Crag Trail, negotiated it by flashlight, and arrived at the road again by 7. A Stop at Conway Cafe, where we got excellent service, and back to MIT by ll P.M, A fun, hard, spirited hike, although short of a summit. The | beginners along did surprisingly well, showing real spirit, climbing trees in Korean boots. John Yates, Gardner and Bob Koppe left Ivy and me (to get gas) and Climbed the peak on Thurgday. It was definitely a "head-in-the-clouds" type of day on top plus "rime ice in your beard." Ivy managed to fall in the brook so we added a new pair of sneakers to the gas. On Thursday we were joined by Doug and Barney who told us the Sad score of the seventh Series game. (Our transistor had simply refused to "transist. The next day they too climbéd the mountain despite pea soup above timberline, Then sometime late Friday night Phil Stevenson arrived with Irene and Merrill from Wheaton and Chris from Simmons. A big vote of thanks to all of them for devoting their efforts to helping Gardner, Bob and John chop and lug trees for the bridge. During that procedure we were royally entertained by successful attempts to cross the waterfall monkey-fashion on the first lone log with arms and legs wrapped hopefully around same. Then ensurd a splash party with Bob heaving large rocks to one gide for the foundation. Saturday evening after supper, Gardner looked up at the sky and predicted precip by morning, so Irene and Chris, John, Gardner, Ivy and I packed up our duds and squeezed into the squareback for a midnight jaunt home. | In addition to the moose which ambled along the trail and practically through camp, we also saw a doe and a fox...plus a persistent little chip- | monk which Ivy took delight in feeding brownies. Trips are run for the benefit of club members. The knowledge or experiences gained on trips are of value to all members of the club. These should be reported on as well as items of practical interest such as meals which succeeded or failed, techniques used, and mistakes made. a. oe ee ee The Saga of Mt. Hale The great Mt. Hale is a mighty 4000 footer in the White Mounatins. The trail to the summit has not been maintained since 1960, although some trail markers remain in the lower stretch. In December of 1970 Noel Morris made it his self appointed task to scale the peak for the glory of MITOC, and proceeded to organize a club trip for that purpose late in December. On about the 20th he and a small group parked approximately near the probable start of the trail and spent the day trying to find it. The possible beginning of the trail was finally found,and a tentative route pushed part of a mile up it before the group was: forced by darkness to retire. The second attempt took place very early in January. The group misplaced | the previous trail but by a bushwack came back to the earlier laid trail at precisely the point where they had been forced to turn back before, at a prominent landmark aptly named "the stove." Pushing eagerly beyond they

MITOC GNARMPFSK 3 March 12, 1971 ascended up a small ridge and were forced to turn back by darkness, determined to return. | Soon after, another attempt was made, and failed almost from the start. Part of the group, desiring to save time, stayed the night in the cabin, planning to meet the other group in the morning. Because of sleeping too late and taking the wrong route to the base of the climb, the two groups met at 11:00 in the morning, too late to start. The rest of the day was spent in climbing Cherry Mountain (an insignificant bump) and in sampling the cuisine of several different restaurants on the way back. Noel's dream was Still stifled. This set the stage for the last and greatest attempt, in mid-February. The intrepid group get an early start and easily pushed up to the previous high spot. They then lost the trail and began a semi-arduous diagonal ascent, pushing straight for the top. Gaining a ridge, the previously scant fog became so thick as to drastically limit vision, and the group Started an arduous bushwack along the ridge. (Flippant comment by someone: "You missed nine thickets back there, Noel," answer: " At last the ridge began to ascend again, the pine becoming denser than ever. A short 60° slope was climbed, and the terrain became alternately regions of scruf brush and thick pine. Suddenly, there was no more ground above us, and we were at the top. The fog lifted, showing a heart wrenching view: two peaks half a mile across a Col from us, and slightly higher. We had missed Mt. Hale, and climbed an insignificant bump beside it (though almost as high) which Noel promptly named "Mt. Shit." The group descended with despair in their hearts, robbed of the goal they had strived so hard for. Memories of the ironic McKinley Sourdough Expedition came to mind, and footsteps were not light. But do not fear, Hale will be climbed, but there are always limitations. It was said, "T am sorry that I have but two days a week to give to Mount Hale." (quotation unclaimed) | Pete King ( |

MITOC GNARM PFSK 5 | March 12, 1971 _The High Cost of Driving _ Most club members seem to be unaware of the fact that the cars used on club trips get pretty well beat up by such use. On a typical trip. the driver averages 350 miles with an average of 2.0 passengers. This means the driver receives $12.25 according to the old club rate (1¢/person/mile including driver). The AAA estimate for operating a car in the northeast 1s 12¢/mile. Thus the driver subsidizes the club to the tune of 29.75 per trip. | More realistically, however, if we consider the actual per mile cost of a trip to the driver, not including the expenses he would ordinarily have to pay for owning the car we still get a rather large sum. Consider my car, the typical gross Americen Car. I pay 3¢/mile for gas, 1.5¢/mile for oil, tune ups, brakes, and tires. 1¢/mile for major repairs such as fuel pump', oil pump, universal joints, ball joints, shock absorbers, etc. More than 1/2 my mileage was put on Club trips. This means the lifetime of my car is reduced by a factor of two. If we assume a Car lasts 70,000 miles and costs $3,500, the cost/mile is 5¢/mile. One half of this is caused by club trips - 2.5¢/mile. Thus my operating costs are 8¢/mile. With a total of 4 people in the car, we get 2¢/person/mile. More economical cars should charge 1.5¢/person/mile. (2¢/mile for gas and 1.5¢/mile for depreciation. The other costs remain about the same.) | How does this translate into cost to club members. A trip to the cabin in an economical car would cost $5.25. In larger Amcrican cars the cost 1s $7.00. Ido not claim that these should be the club rates. Each driver should estimate what these trips cost him and charge accordingly. If a driver does not use his car very often he may not feel that these trips cost him much. Then he will charge 1¢/person/mile and not 1.9 or 2¢. Remember, the only way the club is going to have enough drivers is if these drivers do not lose money on trips. I do not intend nor can I afford to use my car at 1¢/person/mile. Finally, I propose that it is not the driver's responsibility to collect transportation fees. It +s not fair to charge people on the same trip different rates just because they happened to be in an expensive or economical car. Thus the leader should take a weighted average, charge each person equally, and reimburse each driver accordingly. Iam sick of being on trips where some selfish driver sets arate that will cover his cost and not those of another driver and says to the other driver that's too bad. My conscience bothers me (and it should) if Iask my passengers for more. Final apology to non-driver - these rates are SO damn high because it costs so goddamn much to runa car these days. Sorry. I want to hear comments from driver's and suggestions from non-drivers. This problem concerns everybody. Give them to me in writing so I can relay them to the membership. (While any car taken on a trip 4ncurs these expenses, in the case of a car used only on say five trips per year the driver's subsidy of the club is negligible conpared with his own driving expenses, and he easily can afford to x absorb tnese. Costs only become prohibitive when a driver uses his car very often on club tripse)

GNARMPFSK Page 3 , ®ee.ef rom the President' The future development of MITOC has been under consideration for some time. A general feeling has evolved within the club that the quantity of Membership does not necessarily induce the quality of the organization and its activitiese Due to our past inexpensive rental rates on equipment we retary have experienced volume membership without volume participation in club | functions. Last spring, in an effort to eliminate the abuse individuals Were inflicting, the organization initiated a policy which held that equipment Would be rented only to persons participating in a club trip. Unfortunately the previously parasitic members, rather than starting to lead trips or join others have on the most vart simoly become inactive. The absence of these members has had several marked effects? (1) <A decrease in rental, and hence a decrease in profit from rental. (2) A decrease in the membership of undergraduates actively involved in outing club functions. These two consequences are closely related since most graduates are staff members or degree candidates and have been active climbers for many years and also have more money available to purchase eqipment. For many undregraduates MITOC is a new interest and they have not acquired several hundred dollars worth of equipment. Therefore 4t is these beginners who are primarily renting from the clube The importance of involving beginners in the club should not be ignored. It is the new members who are often the most interested in working and therefore the most actives Potentially they are the committed future of MITOC. A quick look at the club reveals that it isn't a student activity. | Rather it is a fraternal organization composed of people who live together, | play together, and spend their weekends together. A beginner is not treated : as a new recruit to keep the sport thriving but more as an intruder into a well ordered societye Is it any wonder we have few if any freshmen among us 7 | There are several things that need to be done in order to change the serious existing conditions. Upon finding it overflowing with people, we unanimously decided to find some other ~ Spot 1n the woods where we could quietly unroll our sleeping bags: We chose the Dolly Copp Picnic Area, and, driving past the "Area Closed after 6 P.M." sign, parlsed the cars next to all the other groups (numbering about 20) who had made the same decision we had. Everywhere we pointed our flashlights, a tent or sleeping bag loomed from the darkness, We finally found an available patch | of ground, It beins clear and warm, we décided to sleep without tents, despite protests from Judy. Shooting stars were seen. The cool morning brought heavy dew. After breakfast, we stuffed our wet sleeping bags and followed our noses to the Berlin paper mill. We drove to what we thought was the head of the Speck Pond Trail, unloaded, and spotted a car at the end of the Goose Eye Trail, Meanwhile, Chuck and Pieter set off to look for the trailhead. The Notch surpassed our expactations, The boulder caves proved to have good acoustics for recorder playing. Packs came off and on several times, and even little Debbie had trouble squeezing through several narrow spots. Chuck amused himself by choosing the hardest routes he could find.

MITOC GNARMPFsK, page 3 Mattawamkeagz, continued Much later that same Monday morning, the canoes and two people were deposited at the appropriate place on the st. Croix. The rest - of the gang took off in search of the place to leave the car for a reunion at the end of the day. This time the delay was caused by Jeannie's muffler falling off, and difficulty in finding the access point to the river, which was down a bunch of obscure logging roads, near @dist-ville. so once again we had memoers of the group going around in circles; meanwhile the two canoe guards passed the time building sand castles. Finally the car was stationed about fifteen miles esac and we set out to run the Croix. at five p.m. Oops! \ Aree no suntan for this day's efforts it was ali we could do to keep out of the cold, ever-lengthening shadows, though I must admit that when we weren't being blinded by the setting sun reflecting off the water we saw some very beautiful Northwoods scenery. The river, WO too, was nice. There was a short portage around Little Falls (in reality just a osg~ rapids under different circumstances we might have tried to run it), and a couple of close calls, but no one really tipped. It's amazing how long the twilight lasts, out the time came when we knew there were plenty of rocks 1mmediately at hand, and we couldn't see them either. so we ferried the canoes over to the other side of the river and pulled them up on shore. But the fun was only just bexinning. Then we had to go looking for the car, wherein were to be found our dry clothes and sleeping bases. According to the maps, the road was maybe a half-mile from the river, Ss2 With the aid of one flashlight we set out to look for it. We stretched out in 2 human chain. leaving off a person at intervals a shouting distance apart as we stumbled with cold feet through the thick undergrowth. When the shouts of the farthest person, John P., were getting faint and the road was not found, we retraced our steps back to the canoes. Since it was to be a day's excursion, we had brought along snacks 'and matches), so we built a fire and sat around it eating gorp and passing hors d'oeuvres trays of crackers laden with cheese, jelly, or peanut butter. It was even proposed that we take off on foot along the river bank in search of the car, but by then we had put the rire to workwarming our bodies (one side at a time), doing 1L0's to alternde sides, and burning our wet tennies, and there seemed to be a good ehance we would survive the night, so we decided to stay put. John re Nancy, and Christy gathered a big supply of firewood, Bruce, Liz, and JE pulled up three canoes for shelter, unwrapped JB's one emergency sleeping bag, got JB, Beannie, Bruce, and Liz stuck under it at random angles, and settled down to sait for morning, which by then . wasn't too far away. Some were waking up-while others were finally falling asleep when it was light enough to renew our quest for the can The ~jround was cold and damp, and the canoes hadn't exactly worked lite reflector ovens, but we took off early with only a little stifimess im the joints as evidence of the night'b trials. MITOC GNARMPFSK, september 1974, pawe 5 PRESIDANTIAL WtisKen D Sunday: Trip to Whitehorse The real rock climbers decided to run a beginner's trip to Whitehorse On Sunday, which is about one hour's drive from the New Cabin. The rumor of a Whitehorse trip immediately attracted Paul Ledoux, and repelled Skip King and John Hollarback who went along anyhow. A carload of Smith girls was enticed into the outing, as well as a girl from B. U. The edbullient Ping from MIT added his effervescence to the group. We split into three ropes of three each. Paul began with a bold lead, a direct line combining the first two pitches. Disdaining even to use his hands, he marched in an upright position up the cliff. He thus exhibited not only his mastery of friction, but also the exces~- Sive number of times he has done the climb. Meanwhile Skip and John had consideably difficulty in one or two spots and swore that the standard Route is highly underrated with respect to the Losemite Apron. Their difficulties and inability with friction were further exasperated when they observed some Appi having an easy time of the route in Black Bastards. Paul tried to trick one of us into doing a 150 foot unprotected lead, but with considerable cursing It backed down and traversed over to the arch. Around the sixth or seventh pich, the weather began looking more and more ominous. It was raining just off to the right, and a strong wind was blowing black clouds in our direction fast. Not relishing the thought of fraction on wet granite, we raced up the remaining pitches. Afterwards we ate pizza in North Conway, and some of the girls tried to outstrip John and 3kip in wit. This was not possible however. The outing was a significant experience for the girls, who were virtually all peginners, and was a gas for the rest of us. The girls in general showed remarkable ability, and with more experience could develop into fine climbers. When we wot to the Bluff it appeared somewhat disappointing, but we went on in, split into 3 groups, and explored it. A presentable route up the left was found, an excellent one in tle center (3 pitches) and a nice one on the right. While it was an excellent place for training the beginners by lunch we were all bored and went wouth a little way. I looked at wagle Cliff, which is across from the Old Man Tourist Trap, and asked if anyone wanted to go have a try at it. Although I was pronounced a harebrained mountaineer by the rock climbers (i. e. them that prefer belaying from the seats of their cars) I got four volunteers (3 beginners and Bill) and we started off. After 15 minutes of hiking up the trail we came to a long set of slabs we third classed Up; then 4 nice technical pitches. We could have gone on slabs all the way to the top, but because of time excaped up a couloir filled with trees to the where we had a magnificent view. The cliff is very large, and presents a wealth of opportunity for new routes, wiftter and summer, all levels of difficulty. The other group looked at another cliff, found it grungy; and salvaged the day with a few stops at bars on the way back. Future climbers can take their pick between the two choices, and have a good time either way. Our major functions are threefold: Trips: MITOC members lead trips throughout the year in a wide range of outdoor activities, including hiking, bicycling, rock/ice climbing, canoeing, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Trips may last anywhere from an afternoon to several months, be composed of a couple or a crowd: participants range from novices to experienced outdoorspeople. a 4 ' > oy 124 North St. Medford, Ma. 02155 ~ ho —S——_— ' * CONSERVATION NEWS: Focus: Pyramid Mall in Attleboro Editor's note: Starting with this issue, we will try to include at least one item of current interest regarding conservation, environmental or ecological issues with each edition of this newsletter. Readers with items to contribute are kindly asked to contact the newsletter editor at club meetings. Thank you. Your help is needed in the fight to save an important piece of Massachusetts wetlands: Michael Deland, Regional Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, has just issued a recommendation to EPA in Washington to prohibit the filling of thirty-two acres of Sweedens Swamp in Attleboro, MA. Sweedens Swamp is a mature red maple wetland of fifty acres which provides excellent habitat for numerous species of birds and small mammals. It is used by migratory waterfowl as well. If upheld by the Washington office, this prohibition will veto a permit that the Army Corps of Engineers has indicated it will issue under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, which regulates dredging and filling activities in wetlands. The Corps decision was made in Washington, and overturned the recommendation of the New England Division of the Corps to deny the permit. The permit is sought by Pyramid Companies of New York to build a large shopping mall. The guidelines to implement Section 404 created a "water dependency test" for wetlands filling projects. If a project is not "water dependent" (for example, a shopping mall), the guidelines presume that an alternative nonwetlands site exists which would result in less damage to the environment. Under these circumstances, destruction of wetlands should be prohibited. Mr. Deland's recommendation finds the Attleboro Mall project violates the guidelines, in that at least one alternative site exists which would fulfill the basic project purpose, i.e. providing shopping opportunities for the region. Pyramid proposes to create artificial wetlands in a sand and gravel pit three miles offsite as "mitigation" for the destruction of Sweedens Swamp. EPA's final decision in Washington on whether or not to veto the Attleboro Mall will be precedent setting for many future wetlands decisions. Allowing the project to go forward will represent a major reversal of previous wetlands policy: "If you don't have to fill a wetlands, don't." Please write to Administrator Lee Thomas in Washington and urge him to uphold the regional recommendation. Mr. Lee Thomas ~ Administrator Environmental Protection Agency 401 M Street SW Washington DC 20460 The decision will be made soon — time is of the essence. | Thank you for your help! The club's primary purpose is trips. The club also owns equipment which it rents to its members to facilitate those trips. The club office is open on Mondays and Thursdays from about 5:00 to 6:00. and is run entirely by volunteers. How to Run a Trip 1. Pick someplace to go. If you can't think of any place in particular, ask someone standing around in the club office. You don't need to have been there before to run the trip. There is no minimum in spectacularity for a trip to be worthwhile. It doesn't have to go to any place remote at all. Any one can run most trips (with a few exceptions: Rock climbing, Winter Camping, and Whitewater Canoeing) 2. Announce the trip on the bulletin board. There is a form that you can use if you want, or you can make up your own little poster-like thingy. 3. Establish the method to decide how to get together. Some trips make all of the last minute arrangements by telephone, some are "show and go", and some get arranged at the club meeting preceding the trip. The advantage of running the trip is that you get to say when and where. Official club trips get a price break on rental equipment. Also, in case there is some limiting resource (tents to rent, cars in which to ride) the leader won't get dropped. : 4. Go on the trip. Enjoy yourself. 5. Come back and inflict your knowledge of why one should (or should not) go and try to reenact your adventure, upon hapless persons who wander into the club office. Try to pick someone who is in step one of planning a trip.
