" massachusetts institute of technology (from Mitch) Snow coverage was lousy. Editorials! The following articles do not necessarily reflect the views of MITOC. The following articles are highly abridged versions of longer reports, so that many statements are made here without justification. Those wishing the full details should contact the author. Ancient Forest Rescue Expedition The most profoundly distressing thing I've done this year was to attend this presentation. The Expedition is a group of private citizens from Washington and Oregon who are concerned about the timber industry's clear aim to destroy all of the old-growth forests in the Pacific Northwest. They are taking their case to the nation by means of this presentation, and a massive 750 year-old felled tree on a semi-trailer. This was their message. Less than 10% of the Ancient Forest remains. In 15 years there will be nothing, but in as few as 5 the ecosystem will be completely compromised by fragmentation. The devastation of cléearcutting is pushed to the small trees on high, steep ridges and watersheds. Consequent erosion and soil runoff drains fertility and kills returning salmon in the

j streams. Burning, spraying with weedkiller and application of fertilizer precede monoculture of Douglas fir in 60-year cycles; the diverse gene-pool and habitat are irreparably destroyed. The Forest Service builds logging roads then sells timber at a net loss; it has a mandate for "multiple use of resources." Jobs are a major justification for logging, but most have been lost to automation. 40% of logs are exported to Asia; the Expedition brought their trunk, felled in the Olympic National Forest, from a Japanese pulp mill in Port Angeles, WA. An ex-logger described his love for the forests and the ambivalence among people who have depended on forestry for generations. A woman spoke about legal action anti-logging lawsuits and the endangered Northern Spotted Owl, and direct action - passive civil disobedience. She is one of a group fined $1500 each and now appealing a $50,000 fine from losing a "punitive action" suit taken by a logging company for occupying a machine. She welcomed anyone wishing to hang in trees or lie on logging roads this summer (contact author if interested). Next a singer performed some of his own numbers, both haunting and rabble-rousing, about the forest and the felling. Finally the speaker outlined names and addresses to write to, and the points to make (see author for details). After some questions and suggestions the Expedition left to truck on to New York. To conclude, this mindless destruction is akin to the poaching of African elephants with machine guns. It can only be stopped by national awareness and pressure in Washington. We have to act now. Environmental Action Now First the bad news. One of the achievements of the Reagan Administration was widespread deregulation; after eight years of the resulting free-for-all, the consequences of "environmental deregulation" are clear, and continuing. 1) The Alaskan North Slope is routinely polluted by illegal but unfettered dumping of wastes and equipment onto the fragile tundra. The oil industry now wants to push its exploration into the adjacent Arctic Wildlife Refuge (contact The Last Great Wilderness). 2) The ancient forests of the Pacific Northwest are now to be destroyed to the last standing giant (see above article). 3) Emissions causing acid rain remain unrestricted, due to the "lack of genuine evidence" of damage to forests, lakes, wetlands and air quality from Virginia to Hudson Bay. 4) The insatiable demand for oil will drain domestic supplies in nine more years. Industry wants to drill on the outer continental shelf, off the unique sand-dune ecosystem of the Outer Banks of North Carolina, and the wildiife-rich California coast. 5) Federal nuclear sites are in an advanced state of contamination, disrepair and undisclosed emissions. While the cleanup is too expensive to countenance, future waste disposal policies continue to be mismanaged. 6)Federal Wild Lands in the West continue to be given away for $2.50 per acre for oil shale extraction. Many are resold for up to 1000 times this for real estate (mainly to satisfy condo-mania). 7) The drought of 1988 caused Congress to listen to global warming reports. "Lack of genuine evidence" removes the need for any action on CFC or CO, output. However, in the press at the moment, Dr. James Hansen of NASA Goddard states that his conclusion of such genuine evidence of warming has been summarily altered. In the same way other government agencies responsible for our best interests distort the truth to go against them in the name of development. The Forest Service fells our trees with our money; the Fish and Wildlife Service refuses to declare endangered species; Environmental Impact Statements for oil exploration, roads and dams are routinely rewritten. Shades of 1984. In the unique system of government in the U.S. "big business" Interests have big money and thus "tame" representatives in Washington. Thus it can break written laws, decide our future on the basis of current profits, and silence its opponents. Now the encouraging news: In this unique system of government the people DO have a right to free speech, even if this means that to overcome a big pressure group one needs a bigger pressure group. These are possible courses of action. Direct action - Marches and rallies or passive civil disobedience (e.g. tree-hanging in Washington State). The author, not a U.S. citizen, does not feel strongly enough to risk deportation. Indirect action - joining environmentally active groups (see author for details). Grass roots - the most effective protest remains the (rationally worded) letter to your senator or representative. For names, addresses and specific points to make, again contact the author. Finally, I'd like to hear from anyone interested in carrying the crusade to the rest of the M.1.T. Community. Bruce Normand Ashdown House 515B 225-9838 This is the MIT Outing Club newsletter. 1nekgT1o1wy2BfubHuauiRd-bWXEpn4lT: = Pa MAT OUTING CLUAR JUNE Ft FFP Hello to all old and new members. Gnarmpfsk is the MIT Outing Club journal of all things worth writing about. The name comes from a contest announced 51 October 1955 and won by one Jim Waters: MITOC's oral tradition teaches that "Gnarmpfsk" is the sound made by a newly-awoken hiker in a wet sleeping bag on a frosty morning, as he ca realizes that if he is to have any hot chocolate he is going to Nave to get up and make it himself. Cabin Log Camelot: The Outing Club's remaining cabin ("Camelot", in Rumney NH) remains un-burned-down. In order to preserve it in this admirable condition, all groups using the Cabin must be accompanied by a Camelot Keyholder. Keyholders are just those people who have gone on a Keyholder Check-out trip (next one, July 24-25; see below), on which they have learned how to operate the stoves safely, what supplies and tools are in the cabin and where they are located, what there is to do for fun around the cabin, and so forth. Keyholders have the responsibility to keep an eye out for fire hazards, and the authority to tell groups to correct a hazardous situation. The Keyholder thus helps the group to better enjoy its stay at the cabin, and reduces the risk of damage to the cabin. If you are a member of a group which might want to use the cabin this year, or if you just want to find out more about Camelot and enjoy a leisurely weekend in the outdoors, then you should consider coming (n.b. MITOC provides Keyholders to groups lacking them for a $25 gratuity payable to the Keyholder, so becoming a Keyholder could earn you some 3 money). Intervale: A year and a half since MITOC's cabin Intervale near North Conway NH burned down, we have received its insured value of $40,000 from our insurance company. Efforts toward replacing the cabin have now resumed. In the next month we hope to come up with construction designs from the architectural drawings of Intervale Ill. We can then get detailed estimates from our general contractor in North Conway, and with a good measure of luck, we will be able to get a weathertight outer structure up by winter. This will necessitate removing the rubble from the current site and replacing at least part of the concrete foundation. Given our constraints, this work will be most efficiently done by the contractor, but there will certainly be the oportunity for MITOC hands to help out with labour during construction of the cabin's frame. Work trips will be organized and advertised in the fall-- watch for them! Further discussion and decision-making regarding Intervale will take place at BOD meetings, so come along and join the exciting deliberations!

= 971 The Yurt: Yurts were invented by Mongolians who needed temporary shelters that could be quickly built. They were modified by quasiindigent Americans who needed permanent shelters that could be cheaply built. They caught the imagination of Dave Maltz (who is neither quasi-indigent nor Mongolian) and so there stands now (6/17) a nearly finished yurt at the MITOC cabin site in Intervale, NH. A yurt is acircular, one-room structure with a skylight at the top, ours is 16° in diamter, and stands 13' at the skylight. It should be open for business after the weekend of July 10-11. We have been lucky that so many people have given their time to help build the yurt. Outreach: The club received a $4,000 grant from Outdoor Nation/Outdoor Foundation and the National Park Service for the development of a 'very MIT' high-­‐school outreach program. Chris Saulnier and Jacob Sargent led the effort to secure the grant. Activities this fall included an overnight trip to the White Mountain National Forest (WMNF) where MITOC leaders Ben Scandella, Sally Miller, Jenn Gagner, and Leigh Ann Kesler partnered with WMNF Rangers to introduce students to current environmental issues facing the Forest (picture below). Adventure Films: Kris Brewer has spearheaded efforts to bring more outdoor adventure films to campus. This fall MITOC hosted the Reel Rock climbing film festival (in conjunction with the Lecture Series Committee) and Pretty Faces, an all female ski film (in conjunction with Graduate Women at MIT). School of Rock: This year marked the launch of a new big event, MITOC's School of Rock. Spearheaded by Dan Weber with the help of many climbing leaders, the program took over 40 MITOCers (out of over a hundred applicants!) through a semester worth of rock climbing related classes. Beginner climbers learned the basics of

belaying, climbing knots, rappelling, ascending the rope, and building top rope anchors. More advanced climbers got to practice placing traditional gear and learn the ins and outs of multipitch climbing. In addition to nighttime lectures and practice, the program included practical outdoor lessons at places like Rumney, Quincy Quarries, and Hammond Pond. The program culminated in an end-­‐of-­‐thesemester trip to the Gunks, where advanced students were able to follow (and in some cases even lead) multipitch trad climbs! Hopefully this is the start of another 45-­‐year tradition like Winter School. Slideshow Socials: Ben Scandella organized a series of weeknight social events in the MITOC office this fall. The events featured free food (always a great way to attract a crowd!) and inspiring pictures on the following subjects: The Quest for the North American Country High Points (Eric and Matthew Gilbertson), Conservation and Photography in the Canyonlands (Harvey Halpern), Iceland (Chris Giebe, Kayla Meduna, Chris Saulnier, Jeff Cegan, Jerome Michon, Jason Jong, Kelly Kochanski, Michelle O'Donnell, Anna de Regt, and Tom Parr), Himalayas: treks in Pakistan and Nepal (Clint Montague and Katie O'Connor), Ski movie: Days of My Youth (hosted by ski chairs Julian Cooper and Nadya Peek), Mt. Rainier (Sally Miller, Ludwig Schmidt, Leigh Ann Kesler, Margie Root, Anna de Regt, and Wolfram Moebius) Winter School: This year, for the 45th winter school, we have over 90 trip leaders and expect more than 300 participants in January. David Lawrence (a.k.a. DLaw) is in charge, assisted by Winter Safety Committee members Nadya Peek, Ben Scandella, and Dan Weber. On December 5th (in unexpectedly snowy conditions!) we had a fun and educational retreat for 40 new leaders at the Camelot cabin. David Cain created a new lottery-­‐based system for trip signups that we hope will minimize frustration for participants who would like to sign up for highly contested trips. Cabins: In addition to regular maintenance at Camelot, cabin manager Pavel Gorelik has pursued two larger scale projects this past year. One was to upgrade the electric service, the other was to repair the roof. We moved the electric meter to a remote pedestal and had the utility company install a new, more powerful, transformer on the pole. The cabin now gets power from the meter via a buried conduit that is less susceptible to damage from tree-­‐fall. The new connection allows for higher amperage at the cabin and provides an independent disconnection means that improves safety when working on the cabin wiring. The service also has room for expansion to accommodate an additional independent 200A circuit for future buildings. We also now have permanent power at the shed and at the water pump.

The second major project was to repair a roof leak that sprung around the chimney a couple years ago. The leak was caused by improper flashing while installing a home-­‐made snow break. The break proved ineffectual at shielding the chimney from snow loads while allowing water to seep in. This fall we installed a significantly taller commercial snow deflector, repaired some water damage and installed a better flashing system. We also extended the chimney by 4', which should provide additional air draw for the stove. Inside the cabin, we replaced all the stove pipe components with higher quality parts. Cabin manager Jenn Gagner executed a major improvement at the Intervale property this year. The old yurt, which was built as a temporary structure between Intervale II and III, was finally razed and replace with a new yurt from White Mountain Yurts. The new yurt is well insulated and includes a proper door, windows, and a skylight with ventilation. The new yurt has neither heat nor artificial lighting, but the improved insulation and windows make it much cozier than what it replaced. Pictures of the old and new yurts are shown below. Anyone with additional information on the history of the original yurt (or the series of Intervale cabins) should get in touch with Jenn at .

Dear MITOC Alumni, Welcome to the summer edition of the GNARMPFSK newsletter. MITOC has been busy this spring term and we are happy to bring you a short selection of things that have been going on. Please enjoy! - The MITOC Alumni Board Activity Spotlight: Trail Work on the Nineteen Mile Trail From Sally Miller, MITOC President On May 30th, a group of twelve MITOCers grabbed some hard hats, gloves, shovels, and hazel hoes and headed up Nineteen Mile Trail for a trail crew with the Appalachian Mountain Club. We spent the day with crew leader Eric clearing drainages, setting rocks, and brushing to improve the trail. Afterwards, we swam in Nineteen Mile Brook and spent the evening at Intervale. It was a great way to give back to the trails since we benefit from them so much! (photos courtesy of Luc Rocher) About Sally: I'm Sally, and I study mechanical engineering. I like to hike, climb, ski, and mountaineer, and I love hanging out with mountain goats in the Cascades.

Activity Spotlight: Winter School 2015 From Jessica Noss (3 season hiking chair) and David Cain (Website). Winter School 2015 was packed full of activity – winter hiking, skiing, camping, ice climbing, and even a little alpine ice hockey. Check out the Gallery on the MITOC website for all the pictures. (http://mitoc.mit.edu/gallery/main.php) Winter School stats: • 376 participants • 258 participants went on at least one trip • 90 certified leaders • Average of 19 trips per weekend during the month of January Thanks Leaders! We had 69 leaders who led at least one trip. Of those 69 leaders, a great number led trips every weekend. Kayla Meduna "won" Winter School, with a total of 7 trips led. Behind her, Nathan Ickes, Rob Foley, and Zavi Dogic all led 6 trips. Dan Brooks led five, and ten other leaders led a total of 4 trips. New Website use The lottery algorithm ensured that all participants who wanted to go on trips got to participate in Winter School. Our participants and leaders had ~8,500 sessions for a total of 71,000 page views. Expedition Spotlight: Cross country cycling trip From Adam Rosenfield. From July–September 2015, I biked my way across the country for fun and adventure. I made it my goal to bag a number of state high points along the way, and to make it a true coast-to-coast trip, I went from the westernmost point in the continental US — Cape Alava, WA — to the easternmost — Lubec, ME. Biking is such a great way to see the country — you get to experience all of the sights, sounds, and smells of all sorts of different places and environments at a slow enough pace to really take it all in. I met so many wonderful, nice people along the way and would recommend it to anyone in a heartbeat. Some stats: • Total distance: 5,602 miles • Days: 73 • States visited: 21, plus District of Columbia • State high points visited: 13, plus DC • State high points biked up: 8, plus DC Arrival at the easternmost point in the United States, West Quoddy Head in Lubec, Maine. New mailing lists for western US and Europe Several new regional mailing lists have been created to help MITOC members, current and former, link up for adventures. The lists are: mitoc-bayarea@mit.edu for the San Francisco area, mitocsocal@mit.edu for southern California, mitoc-seattle@mit.edu for the Pacific Northwest, and mitocalps@mit.edu for Europe. Subscribe to these lists if you live in or will be visiting the areas covered. Have an idea for another list? It's easy and free to set up. Expedition Spotlight: Grand Canyon kayak trip Alumni Board members Chris Glazner and Greg Wallace completed a self-supported kayak trip down the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon this February. The trip took their group of 9 kayakers (including 7 of Chris's friends from the Washington D.C. area) through some of the biggest, most remote whitewater in the continental US. Each kayaker carried all of the food, camping, and safety equipment necessary for the twelve-day trip inside his or her kayak. Thanks to a tricky eddy line at mile 220 that caught Chris off guard, all 9 members of the party flipped and rolled at least once during the 226-mile trip. The team enjoying Redwall Cavern on day 3. GSC Orientation Hiking Trip On Labor day weekend, MITOC collaborated with the Graduate Student Council (GSC) to run a hiking trip for about eighty new graduate students. We organized two buses to the Ferncroft and Franconia trailheads and organized ten hikes ranging from Lonesome Lake to Franconia ridge. Left: A group of incoming grad students at Lonesome lake on the GSC orientation hike. This group took it easy enjoyed and enjoyed viewing waterfalls, eating a warm lunch and playing Bananagrams at the Lonesome Lake hut while other groups were hustling to make it over Cannon, Franconia ridge, and Passaconaway in time to catch the buses back. News in Brief Camelot: The Camelot managers installed a new 19 kW electric stove in the cabin (picture left). This project required reinforcing the kitchen floor from below, as well as substantial electrical improvements. The new stove is much loved by anyone who has to boil water or cook for a large group. Ongoing projects include upgrading the cabin lights, installing new steel tables in the kitchen, and restoring the sauna to operating status. Intervale: We held two keholder trainings in May and November, did basic maintenance, and purchased a new chainsaw. We saw about 3-4 visits per month throughout the year and are continuing to negotiate and defend access via our right of way to the property. School of Rock: The School's second year was an unfettered success! The group was enthusiastic, and every class was valuable. Many of the participants have expressed excitement about becoming MITOC leaders, and they even climb together now outside of the program! Another cool note: we intentionally accepted a 50/50 split of men and women. Women tended to have better attendance, and it was awesome to be part of a group with so many buff and fun female climbers! Gender diversity for the win! Gear Purchases: We updated a large part of our gear fleet by replacing all of our sleeping bags older than 10 years, replacing the oldest and most problematic stoves with new MSR XGKs, and donating the mouse boots to a homeless shelter and replacing them with Sorels. We also added a few bivy bags, expedition sleeping bags, and above treeline tents. In the future, we're looking at updating our mountaineering boots and backpacks. 3-Season Hiking Leaders: We added about thirty new hiking leaders who helped lead circuses in April, August, September, and October. We also ran a few independent trips; three backpacking trips (Kinsmans, Great Gulf, and Baldface) and one day trip to Mt. Washington. Camp Kesem: MITOC contributed free gear rentals this past summer for a trip with Camp Kesem, a program for children whose parents have cancer. "Thanks to MITOC, we had backpacks, tents, and mats to make this trip possible," recalls organizer Veronika Jedryka. "The teen campers absolutely loved the overnight camping trip as we went on hiking trips, made s'mores, played some games, and told stories by the campfire. This trip strengthened friendships and built new ones that continued throughout the rest of Camp Kesem. At the end of Camp Kesem, multiple people mentioned that the overnight camping trip was their favorite of the week."

Expedition Spotlight: Mt. Rainier In summer 2016, several groups organized unofficial trips to the Cascades, two of which happened to cross paths on Mt. Rainier at Camp Muir on the July 4th weekend and exchanged high fives and MITOC fuel bottles. Left: Rainier summit photo of David Migl, John Romanishin, Ben Eck and (not pictured) Adam Rosenfield, a group that had the dubious distinction being the last party to summit for the day. Highlights included crevasse rescue practice, the natural beauty, and the post-summit Chinese buffet. h Obituary: Gardner Perry III, 10 Dec 1927—26 Oct 2016 I'm very sad to let you know that Gardner Perry passed away on 26 October. Twenty-some of his old Boston area friends had gathered on the 15th of October to welcome Gardner and Mary back east in what had become an annual reunion, always at a favorite Chinese restaurant. As usual, a second gathering was planned for family and friends in upstate NY the next day, though their departure may have been delayed as Gardner was not at all well when he arrived in the Boston area. He looked totally exhausted and less than alert – small wonder; only Gardner, at age 88, would attempt such an ambitious travel schedule. A number of us encouraged him to delay his departure for NY and rest for a day or two before continuing; I'm not actually sure whether that advice was accepted in the end. In any case he did successfully complete his journey home to Driggs, ID, but soon ended up in the hospital where he passed away just 11 days after I had been sitting next to him in Bedford, MA. I had seen Gardner and Mary four or five times in recent years, usually at this same Chinese restaurant, but once for a delightful visit with them in Driggs. It was always wonderful to see them and reminisce over many good years of friendship. I am so thankful that I was able to see GP III that one last time. Gardner had been a legend for decades in the New England outing club and climbing communities. Perhaps most importantly, he worked to develop training programs and enhanced safety standards for both rock climbing and winter mountaineering. Gardner was particularly active with the MIT Outing Club (MITOC), but was well-known by members of college outing clubs throughout the northeast, especially affiliates of the Intercollegiate Outing Club Association (IOCA). He led countless trips, helping to build MITOC's first cabin at Intervale, NH, introducing undergrads, grad students, and young professionals to the joys of the mountains, including hiking, rock climbing, snow shoeing canoeing. Were it not for Gardner, many would never have experienced hiking the Presidentials by full moon, canoeing across Lake George at night and joining a square dance and song fest on Mohican Island, being transported in the back of a hearse in order to join an Outing Club trip, celebrating Thanksgiving at Mt Katahdin, and sleeping overnight, high on a mountain, in an igloo. He was a mentor extraordinaire to hundreds of students who came to enjoy, respect, value, and protect, and share our magnificent wilderness. GP III's affiliation with MIT appears to have begun in the early 1950s (he listed his preferred class year as 1953) and continued at least informally until the late 1960s. He was awarded an S.B. in Course 21B (Humanities and Science) in 1961 and for a number of those years worked in the MIT Department of Meteorology. In the late 1960s he founded a mountaineering equipment store on Commonwealth Avenue in Boston; this endeavor later became the foundation of Eastern Mountain Sports. GPIII later moved to the Seattle area, living for a number of years on Vashon Island in Puget Sound, eventually retiring to Driggs, Idaho. Wherever Gardner moved, he always remained close to the mountains and kept in touch his outing club friends. An annual ritual for Gardner and Mary was the celebration of their wedding anniversary with multiple parties, always highlighting folk singing and both square and contra dancing. Hopefully many of us will find opportunities to gather again, join Mary and all Gardner's family, and fondly remember all the joy which Gardner helped to bring to our lives. Gardner is survived by his wife Mary, his sister Trini, his son GP IV, and his daughter-in-law Toni. Condolences may be sent to Gardner's family via Toni at By Tom Parr, MIT XII (1963), , For the MITOC Alumni Board of Directors

Old Speck is almost 50 miles from Intervale, so the first thing we did after leaving the Gabin was to drive almost 50 miles. (What did you expect we did?) Don had muttered something about the trail being steep but what turned up in Grafton Notch was all shock. The trail had been slashed out six feet wide and can be seen going straight up the side of the mountain, looking rather like an optimistically placed fire-break, or like one of these lanes they clear out for a power line. Certainly, it was not like anything that you would want to snowshoe up. Our predictions of difficulty were not, we proved, unfounded. The trail was like one of the well known members of the WOC - short and wicked. Its a mile and a half long and climbs 2600 feet in this distance. In about 2% hours, we made it up to the cabin, which is about amile from the road. It was locked and sealed, so we ate our lunch on the porch. (In case the fire warden should somehow happen to read this; it appears to be in good shape and no one seems to have broken in this winter.) After this little experiment worked so well, we decided to see just how far we could continue to make our hard won potential energy work for us.
